one_liner: Statically typed, LLVM-JIT-compiled low-level language embedded in LuaJIT; typed fib(34) runs 11x faster than PUC Lua.
what_it_does: Terra is a C-like systems language (static types, manual memory, pointers, structs, SIMD vectors) that uses Lua syntax and lives inside a Lua program. Lua code builds, specializes and JIT-compiles Terra functions at runtime, and the two call each other directly using LuaJIT FFI conversion rules. It runs as a standalone `terra` executable/REPL, can save `.o` files or executables, or can be embedded in C/C++ through terra.h (`terra_init(lua_State*)`, `terra_loadfile`, `terra_dofile`), linking libterra_s.a or terra.dll. It is not a drop-in Lua interpreter: Lua code still runs on the bundled LuaJIT, and only code rewritten as typed Terra functions gets native speed.
how_it_is_fast: Terra functions are statically typed and lowered to LLVM IR, then optimized and JIT-compiled to native code for the host CPU (since 1.2.1 host detection enables all host CPU features, similar to -march=native). This is multi-stage programming: Lua acts as the meta-language that generates specialized code, for example inlining Lua constants as literals and using quotes, escapes and macros. C headers are imported through Clang, so calls into C have no FFI overhead and can be inlined. The surrounding Lua runs on LuaJIT, which is itself 12x PUC Lua on the same benchmark page.
when_to_use: You script in Lua and need a few hot kernels (numeric loops, image or stencil code, DSL backends) at native-C speed without writing a separate C extension.
You need runtime code generation or specialization (autotuners, staged DSLs, generated SIMD kernels) and want LLVM-quality code from a high-level meta-language.
Your host is already LuaJIT-based (Lua 5.1 semantics) and you can ship LLVM in the process or in the build.
Ahead-of-time output is acceptable: Terra can emit `.o` files or executables, which avoids JIT start-up and LLVM at run time.
You need GPU code from the same source: CUDA, with AMD/HIP and experimental Intel SPIR-V on recent LLVM versions.
when_not_to_use: As a faster runtime for existing dynamically typed Lua scripts: untyped Lua code just runs on LuaJIT, so plain LuaJIT (0.111 s vs Terra 0.121 s on the same fib page) gives the same gain without LLVM.
PUC Lua 5.3/5.4 hosts: terra.h includes the bundled LuaJIT's lua.h and terra_init expects a LuaJIT state, so Terra cannot be added to a stock Lua 5.4 embedding.

Small footprint, sandboxed or JIT-forbidden targets (iOS, consoles, hostile scripts): Terra needs LLVM and Clang (11-22; 15 and older deprecated), generates native code, and gives no memory safety (manual memory and raw pointers).
Windows-centric projects: issue #668 says Terra is looking for Windows maintainers, and the static-library-with-LLVM bundling options are not supported on Windows.
Short scripts where start-up matters: the 0.121 s whole-process figure includes LLVM initialization and JIT compilation, about 0.05 s above MSVC-compiled C (0.074 s) for the same fib.

integration.dependencies: LLVM and Clang 11-22 (22 recommended, 11-15 deprecated), LuaJIT (downloaded and built automatically), CMake 3.26.4+, GNU Make on Unix; optional CUDA
integration.min_toolchain: C++17 compiler; Visual Studio 2022 on Windows; CMake 3.26.4
integration.platforms: Linux x86-64, AArch64, PPC64le; macOS x86-64 and AArch64; FreeBSD x86-64; Windows x86-64; GPU targets NVIDIA CUDA, AMD HIP, Intel SPIR-V (experimental)
integration.thread_safety: not documented in the README; each embedding owns a LuaJIT lua_State, which is single-threaded as in Lua. A multiterra.t test exists and fails on PPC64le (issue #583).

gotchas: Benchmark harness: Scriptorium's tests/fib.t is a typed `terra fib(a : int) : int` compiled by LLVM, while tests/fib.lua is a dynamically typed function run by the PUC interpreter. The 11x compares a compiled language with an interpreter, not two script engines. bench.cc times whole `system()` runs, including LLVM start-up, with no fib(0) overhead subtracted (`overhead = 0`) and no check of program output. Terra's three bench.csv runs (0.124, 0.121, 0.124 s) are consistent.

JIT performance depends on the LLVM version: release 1.2.2 (2026-08-14) notes 'Restore the manual inliner for JIT mode on LLVM 17+', so 1.2.0 and 1.2.1 builds against LLVM 17+ JIT-compiled without Terra's inliner.

JIT code targets all host CPU features by default (1.2.1+). Objects or executables saved for distribution need an explicit target, and choosing a default triple and architecture is still an open issue (#633).

Open crash reports cover embedding (#516, assertion `!lua_isnil(L->L, -1)` failed), segfaults after disassembling code (#450) and with the Vulkan API on prebuilt Linux binaries (#487), and failures on PPC64le (#583, #581, Moonjit bugs).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Terra over Daslang, Chibi-Scheme, Pawn, TinyVM or c4x86 when you want native LLVM-optimized code generated from Lua meta-programs and can afford an LLVM dependency. For faster ordinary game scripting without LLVM, Daslang or LuaJIT-family engines such as LuaJIT Remake are lighter. On this exact page, c4x86 (0.136 s) is close to Terra with no LLVM at all.
verified_claims_summary: In r-lyeh's Scriptorium (July 2015; AMD A10 3.8 GHz, Windows 7 64-bit; build flags and Terra version not stated, linked as zdevito/terra), recursive fib(34) took 0.121 s for Terra against 1.341 s for the PUC Lua interpreter: 11x as whole-process wall time, best of repeated 5-run averages. LuaJIT (0.111 s) and MSVC C (0.074 s) were faster on the same page.
status_note: Active and MIT-licensed (Stanford): release 1.2.2 on 2026-08-14 added LLVM 19-22 and fixed calling-convention and JIT-inliner regressions, with 2.9k stars, 92 open issues and Windows maintenance asking for help. Usable via binary releases, but plan for a heavyweight LLVM-plus-LuaJIT dependency.
